response_text: Setting up a thread's stack means creating a fake execution context that tricks the processor into believing it's resuming an already-running thread when it's starting for the first time. We manually push register values onto the thread's stack in the exact order ARM processors expect during interrupt returns: xPSR, PC, LR, R12, R3-R0, then R11-R4. The critical values are xPSR (processor status) and PC (set to our thread function address). Everything else gets arbitrary values for debugging. We store register values on the stack because that's how ARM handles context switching. When our system calls switches to the thread's stack and performs an interrupt return, it pops our pre-arranged values into hardware registers. When PC gets popped with our function address, the processor thinks it's continuing interrupted execution but starts our thread. This exploits the normal interrupt mechanism in reverse, bootstrapping thread execution by mimicking the processor's own context-switching behavior.\n
